title: STAT+: Medicare estimates $9.2 billion in savings from third round of negotiated drug prices
summary: The Trump administration said that the federal government will save $9.2 billion on drugs purchased through Medicare next year as a result of price negotiations.
content: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration on Monday said that the federal government will save $9.2 billion on drugs purchased through Medicare next year as a result of price negotiations, a net savings of 45% compared to what it would’ve paid last year had the negotiated prices been in effect. This is the third time the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has negotiated drug prices following the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act, but it’s the first time those drugs have included treatments administered in doctors’ offices , which are covered by Part B. Only retail drugs covered by Part D were eligible during the first two years. The estimated $9.2 billion in savings does not account for discounts the drugmakers pay to the Part D Manufacturer Discount Program. That program was created by the same law that established the price negotiation program. If those discounts were included, the estimated savings would be about $5.5 billion, or 33% in lower net aggregate spending. Continue to STAT+ to read the full story…

title: How artificial intelligence is offering new hope for stroke patients in the Last Frontier
summary: In Alaska, a small network of hospitals is betting on AI tools to triage stroke patients and get them to the right care, faster.
content: It was just after lunchtime when the doctor’s phone started to vibrate and chime. On this summer Wednesday, a neurointerventionalist in Anchorage got the alert: Three hundred miles away, at a hospital deep in Alaska’s interior, a clot in a major artery was blocking the flow of blood to a patient’s brain. He needed it out — and he’d have to come to the state’s biggest city to get it done. Time is never on a stroke patient’s side. Every minute without blood flow, 2 million brain cells die. And in Alaska — a state more than double the size of Texas, most of it inaccessible by road — it can take several hours to arrange a plane, airlift a patient to Ted Stevens airport in Anchorage, and deliver them by ambulance to one of the five neurointerventionalists in the entire state who can extract clots. Read the rest…

title: STAT+: AI can analyze X-rays and CT scans to draft radiology reports. Will it make care better, safer?
summary: As the Radiological Society of North America meets in Chicago, industry insiders are expected to debate if AI draft reporting will improve care.
content: For more than two decades, artificial intelligence has played a growing role in the practice of radiology. Today, nearly every radiologist uses AI tools, whether that’s to triage the images they interpret, dictate their reports, or detect findings in the dozens of X-rays and CTs they read every day. But last year, radiology experts and developers at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America began to foreground a new paradigm in AI. Business acquisitions and debates centered on technology, powered by vision-language models, that can do the core work of a radiologist: looking at an image, and drafting a report of the clinical findings within it. “Last year’s RSNA was mainly focused on whether it’s actually possible that an AI model will write a draft for radiologists that would look like an actual radiology report, and that would be accurate enough to be even considered by a radiologist,” said Michael Braginsky, chief technology officer of Aidoc. Continue to STAT+ to read the full story…

title: Opinion: Genomic testing is too fragmented. Instead, we should test once and evaluate often
summary: “It’s time to consolidate testing by sequencing genomes once and reevaluating them when needed,” a genetic counselor writes.
content: Genomic testing can answer a variety of pressing health questions a person (and their clinician) might face throughout their lifespan. Unfortunately, these valuable tests have become fragmented and iterative for most patients. A patient may receive a carrier screening test before or during pregnancy; a cancer predisposition test to screen for inherited cancer-predisposition variants like BRCA, the breast cancer gene; and a pharmacogenomic test before starting a medication. Each test is a new blood draw or buccal swab, a new wet lab workflow, a new spot on a genome sequencer, a new analysis, and new costs borne by patients and insurance companies. Read the rest…

title: Opinion: Why medical students should keep going to class
summary: “Attending lectures in person has become … the most powerful way I take care of my mental health,” medical student Brian Zhang writes.
content: This article is part of a new First Opinion series on the future of medical school. By this time of year, the sky is black when I step outside. The day has carried me from lectures on gastrointestinal cancer disparities to TAing microbiology, from student government debates to helping free-clinic patients complete paperwork for expensive medications. With the cold nipping at my skin, I look back at the Stanford medical school building, its windows glowing. There is still so much to do, and even more to feel. I call my mother, my home base in human form. Three thousand miles away, she is preparing for bed. Circumstances beyond her control have kept her from taking a domestic flight for decades, let alone visit me in California. Her first question is always, “Did you remember to eat dinner?” Her second: “How were your classes today?” Read the rest…

title: STAT+: RFK Jr. spills his calendar into public, but leaves much to the imagination
summary: A partially redacted calendar showing health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s activities was made public on Tuesday.
content: WASHINGTON — A new website launched by the Trump administration provides centralized access to more than 92,000 public records from the Department of Health and Human Services and the agencies it oversees — including partially redacted entries from health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s calendar. While many of the records were previously available, the health department heralded the launch of the site as a sign of its “radical transparency.” In June, after a New York Times report referred to him as disengaged with the job, Kennedy said on social media that his calendar was publicly available, though no such calendar had been made available for the media or the public before Tuesday. A number of Freedom of Information Act requests filed by STAT reporters had previously gone unanswered and even unacknowledged and do not appear to be included in the Tuesday release. Much of the secretary’s partial calendar, which reflects his activities from Feb. 13, 2025, to June 19, 2026, is redacted, including some private calls taken by the secretary. One of his closest aides at the agency, Stefanie Spear, appears to be listed only once in the calendar. References to other notable meetings are not redacted, including one that would ultimately lead to the ouster of a short-lived director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Susan Monarez. Continue to STAT+ to read the full story…

title: STAT+: Sanofi to buy Insmed for $41B, picking up two lung disease medicines
summary: Sanofi is buying U.S. biotech Insmed for $41 billion, a megadeal that will give the French pharma company two new approved medicines.
content: Sanofi is buying the biotech Insmed for $41 billion, the companies said Tuesday, the largest biopharma acquisition in years and one that will give the French firm two new approved drugs. The purchase, which includes another drug in Phase 3 trials, reflects the pressure Sanofi has been under as it faces looming revenue losses from its massive blockbuster Dupixent, an inflammation-targeting drug approved in nine indications. The company, where Belén Garijo took over as CEO earlier this year, had been vocal that it was looking for takeover targets with late-stage or even commercial assets that fit with its existing focus in immunology and rare diseases. Sanofi is paying $175 per share for New Jersey-based Insmed, through a combination of debt financing and cash. Insmed’s share price was roughly $120 before Bloomberg reported last week that the deal was in the works, which sent the stock up. Continue to STAT+ to read the full story…

title: STAT+: In a rare move, the FDA cites two drugmakers for failing to report clinical trial results to a database
summary: For the first time in more than a year, the FDA sent notices to companies for failing to report required clinical trial information.
content: For the first time in more than a year, the Food and Drug Administration has sent notices to companies for failing to report required clinical trial information. The agency sends such notices when a trial sponsor fails to comply with a federal law that requires studies to be registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, a federal government database, within 21 days after the first human subject is enrolled. Summary results must also be posted to the database within 12 months after the trial’s primary completion date. The FDA, however, has rarely sent noncompliance letters, despite years of criticism over lax enforcement. In recent years, calls for greater transparency have sparked a raft of studies showing a failure by drug companies, universities, and academic medical centers to comply with disclosure requirements. title: STAT+: Pharmalittle: We’re reading about Sanofi buying Insmed, Roche touting its breast cancer pill, and more
summary: Sanofi is buying the biotech Insmed for $41 billion, the largest biopharma acquisition in years and one that will give the French firm two new approved drugs
content: Hello there from STAT’s London bureau, with reporter Andrew Joseph here filling in for Mr. Pharmalot for a few days. It may be a holiday week stateside, but the news, at least for now, has yet to let up. So grab your choice cup of stimulation and settle in. … Sanofi is buying the biotech Insmed for $41 billion, the largest biopharma acquisition in years and one that will give the French firm two new approved drugs , STAT tells us. The purchase, which includes another drug in Phase 3 trials, reflects the pressure Sanofi has been under as it faces looming revenue losses from its blockbuster inflammatory drug Dupixent. Sanofi has been upfront that it was searching for takeover targets with late-stage or clinical assets, and with the deal, it will get New Jersey-based Insmed’s two lung disease drugs. Roche touted the blockbuster potential of a new breast cancer pill after winning two U.S. regulatory approvals within a week , Bloomberg shares. The new medicine, called Wilserdly, is central to the drugmaker’s plan to regain its footing in the fast-growing cancer market. The company is positioning the pill to replace decades-old hormone therapies that are taken for years in an effort to reduce the risk the cancer will return. Estimates from analysts placing its peak annual sales potential at $9 billion are roughly in line with its own expectations, the Swiss drugmaker said. Continue to STAT+ to read the full story…
